chunks: Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Masrur, may Allah be pleased with him, told us. He said: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn 'Amir told us, from his paternal uncle 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir, from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibrahim al-Karkhi, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) that he said:

A narration that you comprehend is better than a thousand narrations which you narrate. A man from you will not be knowledgeable (faqih) until he is aware of the various indications (ma'arid) of our speech. Verily, the word from our speech does indeed turn to seventy indications, all of which we may intend.

key_terms.سَبْعِينَ وَجْهًا: Seventy faces or aspects, referring to the multiplicity of meanings in a single statement
key_terms.فَقِيهًا: A knowledgeable jurist or scholar who understands the depths of religious knowledge
key_terms.مَعَارِضَ: Indications, nuances, or multiple facets of meaning in speech

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between a simple narrator and a true faqih according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith, foundational to the book *Mani al-Akhbar*, establishes that true jurisprudence requires mastering the art of interpreting the Imams' speech through its subtle nuances (*ma'arid*) rather than merely accumulating reports. It highlights the hermeneutical depth of Shia scholarship, where a single utterance can encompass up to seventy distinct meanings, reflecting the multifaceted nature of divine guidance. This principle underscores the necessity of contextual and linguistic analysis in deriving legal and theological rulings from the Ahl al-Bayt.
